claims.text: Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a homogeneous grain structure.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive yield strength of 786 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has an approximately 13.5% terminal compressive strain.
Warm rolling below the recrystallization temperature followed by controlled annealing will produce a heterogeneous bimodal grain structure in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Fine grains in the proposed bimodal structure will sustain high strength.
Coarse grains will promote strain partitioning and back-stress hardening.
The bimodal grain structure will delay necking and increase uniform tensile elongation.
Load transfer between fine- and coarse-grained regions will facilitate progressive plasticity.
Dislocation accumulation associated with the heterogeneous structure will contribute to ductility and strain hardening.
Balancing fine- and coarse-grained regions will preserve the alloy's impact-triggered chemical energy release capability.
Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has approximately 13.5% tensile elongation.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation from approximately 13.5% to 18–20%.
The treatment will maintain yield strength within ±10% of 786 MPa.
The treatment will retain similar impact-triggered energy release performance.
The predicted ductility benefit applies to room-temperature tensile loading at strain rates on the order of 10^-3 s^-1.
The treatment's benefits and trade-offs at high strain rates or elevated temperatures are uncertain.
The rolling reduction, rolling temperature, annealing time, and annealing temperature needed to obtain the target microstructure remain undetermined.
Failure to reach 18–20% uniform tensile elongation would falsify the hypothesis.
A yield-strength or impact-energy-release decrease greater than 10% relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is identified as terminal compressive strain in the initial-state field but is reclassified as baseline tensile elongation and uniform tensile elongation elsewhere.

The 786 MPa baseline is explicitly a compressive yield strength, but the predicted outcome and tensile-focused falsification design use it as an apparently tensile yield-strength target without distinguishing loading mode.
